title: RMS and Average Values Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 11
description:
Aarav's room heater is labelled 230 V, but on a scope the mains voltage swings up to about 325 V and down to -325 V. So which number is the real voltage? Both are real. They are different kinds of values, and this animated lesson shows exactly what each one means.

On a live breadboard, the same heater coil runs on an alternating supply and on a battery. We turn the battery up until both coils make the same heat every second: that steady DC is the RMS value, 0.707 of the peak. We derive Vrms = Vm/root 2 step by step (square, mean, root), flatten one hump of the wave to find the half-cycle average 2Vm/pi = 0.637 Vm, and meet the form factor (1.11) and the peak factor (1.414). Then a worked example on the 230 V mains (325 V peak, 207 V average, 650 V peak to peak), the exam trap (full-cycle average is zero), where it is asked, an original JEE Main pattern practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 14 of PUC Electronics, Class 11, Chapter 2: Principles of Electricity, Network Theorems and AC Principles (Karnataka PUC Electronics).

In this video:
0:00 230 V on the label, 325 V on the scope
0:17 Peak, peak to peak and the zero average
0:45 Breadboard: alternating supply vs battery, same heat
1:25 RMS is the steady DC that gives the same heat
1:30 Deriving Vrms = Vm/root 2
2:20 Average value, form factor and peak factor
2:58 Worked example: the 230 V mains
3:27 Exam trap: full cycle vs half cycle
3:46 Where it is asked
3:58 Practice question
4:33 Formula card
